NMOS and PMOS differential pairs in parallel so that one works when the other turns off near a rail, extending the input common-mode range to both supplies.
A small circuit that injects current into a self-biased reference at power-up so it cannot remain in its zero-current (degenerate) operating point, and then turns itself off.
A loop of two current mirrors whose reference current is a copy of its own output, with a resistor that fixes the current level, making the current nearly independent of the supply voltage.

A bias scheme in which the transconductance of the biased transistors is set by a resistor ($g_m = \frac{2}{R_S}(1 - 1/\sqrt{K})$) rather than by mobility or threshold, keeping $g_m$ stable over process and temperature.
Techniques that cancel the second-order temperature dependence (bowing) left in a first-order bandgap reference, which comes mainly from the non-linear temperature dependence of $V_{BE}$.
A bandgap reference that adds a PTAT current and a CTAT current and converts the sum to a voltage with a resistor, so its output (and supply) can be well below the 1.2 V of a classic bandgap.

The bipolar transistor available in a standard n-well CMOS process: p+ diffusion as emitter, n-well as base and the grounded p-substrate as collector. It provides the junctions for CMOS bandgap references.
The error step coupled onto a sampling capacitor by the clock edge through a switch's gate overlap capacitance; roughly $V_{CK}WC_{ov}/(WC_{ov} + C_H)$ and independent of the signal.
A half-width transistor with source and drain shorted, clocked opposite to a sampling switch, that absorbs the channel charge the switch injects and cancels its clock feedthrough.

Switching scheme in which the switch at the op-amp (virtual-ground) side of the sampling capacitor opens first, so its signal-independent charge sets the sample and later switches cannot disturb the stored charge; the capacitor's bottom plate is kept on driven nodes.

A switched-capacitor sample-and-hold that samples the input on a capacitor with the op amp in unity feedback and then flips the capacitor around the op amp, giving an output equal to the sampled input with input-independent charge injection.
An integrator in which a capacitor switched between the input and the op amp's virtual ground replaces the input resistor, adding $(C_1/C_2)V_{in}$ to the output each clock period.
A capacitor alternately connected to two nodes at a clock rate $f_{CK}$; it moves an average current $C_Sf_{CK}(V_A - V_B)$ and so behaves like a resistor $1/(C_Sf_{CK})$.

A switched-capacitor stage in which two equal capacitors sample the input and one is then placed in feedback while the other dumps its charge into it, giving a gain of two with a feedback factor near one half.
The frequency at which the loop-gain magnitude $|\beta H|$ falls to one (0 dB); the phase margin is read there.
The frequency at which the loop-gain phase reaches $-180^{\circ}$; a stable loop has its gain below one there.
The paths traced in the s-plane by a feedback system's closed-loop poles as the loop gain is varied.
Lowering an amplifier's dominant pole (for example with load capacitance) until the gain crosses unity near or below the first non-dominant pole, giving adequate phase margin.
A closely spaced pole and zero, typically from imperfect pole-zero cancellation, which leaves a slow, small-amplitude tail in the step response.
Compensation in which the Miller capacitor returns output current through a common-gate transistor to the first-stage node, so no feedforward path exists and the right-half-plane zero disappears.
Connecting the compensation capacitor from the output to the low-impedance source of the first stage's cascode transistor, raising both the zero and the non-dominant pole.
An open-loop-stable feedback system is stable if and only if the polar plot of $\beta H(s)$ around the right half plane does not encircle $-1$.
If a closed contour encloses Z zeros and P poles of F(s) clockwise, the image of the contour under F encircles the origin Z minus P times clockwise.
Stability that holds only for a band of loop gains, so that reducing the gain (not only raising it) can make the loop oscillate; it arises when the phase crosses -180 degrees several times.
The empirical rule that the random mismatch between two identically drawn transistors falls with the square root of their area: $\sigma(\Delta V_{TH}) = A_{VTH}/\sqrt{WL}$.
Techniques that measure an amplifier's offset in a dedicated clock phase, store it on capacitors and subtract it during normal operation; they also suppress low-frequency noise.
Taking two closely spaced samples, the first of the offset or reset level and the second of the signal, and subtracting them, so that offset and noise slower than the sample spacing cancel.
Linearization by following a nonlinear V-to-I stage with an I-to-V stage that has the inverse characteristic, such as a square-law differential pair loaded by diode-connected square-law devices.
The dependence of a capacitor's value on its voltage, which makes stored charge a nonlinear function of voltage and distorts switched-capacitor circuits whose gain is not one.

Sizing method for short-channel devices: simulate one reference transistor's $I_D$, $g_m$ and $r_O$ once, then obtain each circuit device by scaling its width and current by the same factor at the same overdrive.
Drain current per unit width, $I_D/W$. Scaling width and current together keeps it, the overdrive and $g_m/I_D$ constant, so $g_m$ scales linearly with the width.
The fractional difference between a feedback amplifier's actual closed-loop gain and its ideal ratio, about $1/(\beta A_0)$ for open-loop gain $A_0$ and feedback factor $\beta$.

The requirement that the common-mode feedback loop of a fully differential op amp be stable on its own; its loop gain is measured with the differential feedback in place and is often compensated with a capacitor at the error amplifier's output.
The area where a tyre touches the road, roughly the size of a hand on a car. Every braking, cornering and driving force passes through the four contact patches.

The ratio of the friction force between two surfaces to the force pressing them together, written $\mu$. For a tyre it sets the most grip it can make: about 0.9 to 1.0 for a road tyre on dry tarmac and 1.4 to 1.7 for a warm racing slick.

The angle between the direction a tyre is pointing and the direction it is actually travelling. A tyre must run at a slip angle to make cornering force; the force peaks at roughly 3 to 8 degrees on a racing slick and falls past that.
How much faster or slower a tyre turns than the road passes under it, as a fraction of road speed. Braking and driving force peak at roughly 10 to 15 percent slip; a locked wheel is 100 percent.
Pacejka's empirical fit to measured tyre force curves, $F = D \sin(C \arctan(B x - E(B x - \arctan(B x))))$, with $x$ the slip angle or slip ratio and $D$ the peak force.

A plot of a car's braking or accelerating force against its cornering force. Its edge is the grip limit: grip used for braking cannot also be used for turning, so a fast driver blends one into the other along the edge.
The fall in a tyre's friction coefficient as the load on it rises: doubling the load less than doubles the grip. It is why weight transfer across an axle reduces that axle's total grip.
The movement of load between the tyres when a car brakes, accelerates or corners, because its centre of mass sits above the road. For braking at $a$ the load moved to the front axle is $m a h / L$.
The point at which a body's mass can be treated as concentrated. On a car, the higher it is, the more weight transfers in braking, accelerating and cornering.
The distance between the front and rear axles. A longer wheelbase means less longitudinal weight transfer and a more stable but less agile car.
The distance between the left and right wheels on one axle. A wider track means less lateral weight transfer in corners.
Handling in which the front tyres reach their grip limit first, so the car turns less than the steering asks and runs wide. Also called push or a tight car.
Handling in which the rear tyres reach their grip limit first, so the rear steps out and the car turns more than the steering asks. Also called a loose car.
Oversteer caused by lifting off the throttle in a corner: load moves forward, the rear tyres lose grip and the tail swings out.
Oversteer caused by too much throttle, which makes the driven rear tyres spin and lose their cornering grip.
Aerodynamic force from wings and a shaped floor that pushes a car onto the road, adding grip without adding mass. It grows with the square of speed.
The air's resistance to a car's motion, growing with the square of speed. Wings that add downforce also add drag, which lowers top speed.
The disturbed, slower air behind a car. A car following closely in it loses downforce in corners but gains a slipstream on straights.
The loss of a tyre's grip over a stint as it wears and overheats, which makes lap times rise.
Small rolls of rubber torn off a tyre that slides while too cold; they sit on the tread and reduce grip until worn away.
Bubbles of rubber lifting from a tyre's tread when it overheats from inside, which ruins its grip.
A racing tyre with no tread, giving the largest contact patch on a dry track. Unusable in standing water.
The path round a track that gives the lowest lap time: normally outside, inside at the apex, and outside again, adjusted to give the best exit onto the straights.
The point where a car's path comes closest to the inside of a corner, usually touching the inside kerb.
A line that turns in later and touches the inside further round a corner than the geometric line, trading some speed in the corner for an earlier, straighter exit.
Touching the inside of a corner too soon, which leaves too much turning to do afterwards and makes the car run out of track on the exit.
The single constant-radius arc through a corner that uses the full width of the track. It gives the highest minimum speed but rarely the fastest exit.
The point where a driver begins steering into a corner.
The point after a corner where the car reaches the outside edge of the track as the steering unwinds.
Where a driver starts braking for a corner, usually marked by a reference such as a braking board.
A visible landmark (a board, kerb, crack or mark) a driver uses to brake, turn in or apex at the same place every lap.
A slow corner that turns through about 180 degrees.
A quick sequence of corners in opposite directions, often added to slow cars before a fast section.
A corner that gets tighter as it goes, so its apex is later than it first looks.
A corner whose surface slopes down towards the outside, which reduces grip.
The edges of the track a car must stay within. Usually the white edge lines count as track and the kerbs beyond them do not. Running wide to gain time is penalised.
Braking at the highest force the tyres allow without locking the wheels.
Carrying brake pressure past the turn-in point and releasing it gradually as steering is added, keeping the tyres on the edge of the friction circle and load on the front tyres.
A system that pulses brake pressure to stop the wheels locking, so the car can still steer under hard braking.
A system that cuts engine power when the driven wheels start to spin.
A system that brakes individual wheels to stop a car sliding. Common on road cars and as an aid in racing games; rare in racing.
Braking with the ball of the right foot while blipping the throttle with the heel or side of the same foot, so a downshift can be rev-matched during braking.
Raising the engine speed during a downshift to match the lower gear, so the driven wheels are not jolted or locked when the clutch engages.
Steering in the direction the rear of the car is sliding to catch oversteer.
Changing up a gear before the usual shift point, to send less torque to the wheels and reduce wheelspin, or to save fuel.
Driven wheels turning faster than the road under them because of too much throttle, which costs grip and acceleration.
A wheel that stops rotating under braking and slides, losing steering and some stopping grip and flat-spotting the tyre.
The adjustments made to a car for a track, conditions and driver: tyre pressures, alignment, springs, dampers, anti-roll bars, aerodynamics, differential, gearing and brake bias.
The tilt of a wheel seen from the front. Negative camber, top leaning in, keeps the tyre flatter on the road as the car rolls in a corner.
Whether a car's wheels point in (toe-in) or out (toe-out) seen from above. Front toe-out sharpens turn-in; rear toe-in adds stability.
The backward tilt of the steering axis, which gives self-centring and steering weight.
A torsion bar linking the left and right wheels that resists body roll. A stiffer front bar adds understeer; a stiffer rear bar adds oversteer.
A suspension part that resists motion in proportion to its speed, controlling how fast weight transfers. Bump damping resists compression; rebound resists extension.
The height of a car's body or floor above the road. Lower lowers the centre of mass and can add floor downforce.
The difference between rear and front ride height. More rake (rear higher) usually moves the aerodynamic balance forward.
The share of a car's downforce on the front axle. More at the front adds front grip and oversteer in fast corners.
A differential that partly locks the two driven wheels together so power is not lost to the unloaded inside wheel.
A base amount of locking in a limited-slip differential that acts at all times.
The ratio that scales all the gears of a car together, trading acceleration for top speed.
The ratio of engine speed to wheel speed in a gear. Shorter gearing gives harder acceleration and a lower top speed.
The share of braking force at the front axle, typically 55 to 70 percent. More front bias is stable but understeers on entry; more rear bias helps rotation but risks spinning.
The air pressure in a tyre, which rises as it warms. The hot pressure sets the contact patch shape and the tyre's grip.
The rubber mix of a tyre. Softer compounds grip more but wear and overheat sooner.
Adjustments (weight, power, air restrictors) that racing organisers or games apply to make different car models equally fast in one class.
Extra weight added to a car to meet a minimum weight, balance its handling, or slow it down under a balance of performance or success rule.
The low-drag region behind a moving car. A car following closely in it can go faster on a straight and use the extra speed to overtake.
An overtaking aid that opens a flap in the rear wing to cut drag for a car close behind another in a set zone.
An overtaking aid giving a short burst of extra engine power a limited number of times per race.
Getting past another car, most often on the inside under braking after following it in the slipstream.
Overtaking by braking later than the car ahead into a corner. Legitimate only if the attacker can still make the corner.
An overtaking move in which the attacker goes wide, turns in late behind a defender who has taken the inside, and uses a better exit to pass on the next straight.
Pitting before a rival and using the grip of fresh tyres to gain enough time that the rival comes out behind after their stop.
Staying out longer than a rival who has pitted, gaining while their new tyres warm up or they meet traffic.
A stop in the pit lane for tyres, fuel, repairs or a driver change. With the pit-lane speed limit, a stop often costs 20 to 30 seconds.
The laps a car runs between pit stops, or one driver's spell at the wheel in an endurance race.
Lifting off the throttle a little before the braking point to save fuel and cool the brakes, at a small cost in lap time.
A car that leads the field at reduced speed while an incident is cleared. Gaps close up and a pit stop costs less time.
A flag telling a driver that a faster car is about to lap them and they must let it pass.
A flag warning of danger ahead: slow down and do not overtake.
The black-and-white flag that ends a race or session.
A race start with the cars already moving behind a pace car.
A race start from stationary cars on the grid, released when the start lights go out.
Races lasting several hours, often 6, 12 or 24, with drivers sharing one car.
A race car with its wheels outside the bodywork, usually with large wings, such as Formula 1 and IndyCar cars.
A race car based on a road-going sports car, raced in GT classes often balanced by balance of performance.
Racing one car at a time against the clock on closed roads of tarmac, gravel or snow, with a co-driver reading pace notes.
A rally co-driver's coded description of the road ahead (corner severity, distances, hazards), read aloud to the driver.
A motorsport in which drivers are judged, not timed, on sliding a car sideways with angle, speed and style.
Racing in a computer simulation of real cars and tracks, usually with a steering wheel and pedals, close enough to reality that racing teams use simulators for training.
The recorded data of what a car did through a lap: speed, throttle, brake, steering, gear, accelerations and more, used to compare laps and find time.
The running gap to a reference lap at each point round the track; where it rises steeply is where time is lost.
One of the parts (often three) a lap is divided into for timing.
The sum of a driver's best time in each sector, showing the time available without any new skill.
A see-through replay of a reference lap shown on track in a racing game, to follow or race against.
Forces a sim steering wheel's motor applies to reproduce what the front tyres send up a real steering column; the main way a sim driver feels grip.
A sim brake pedal that measures the force on it rather than its travel, as a real brake does.
The angle of the scene shown on screen. In a sim it should match the angle the screen covers from the driver's eye, $2 \arctan(h / 2d)$ for screen height $h$ at distance $d$.
Systems that make a car easier to drive: ABS, traction control and stability control, and in games also automatic braking, steering help and a drawn racing line.
A family of card games in which players bet on who holds the best hand, and can win without it by betting so that everyone else folds.
The most played form of poker: each player gets two hole cards and shares five community cards, dealt in a flop, turn and river, with four betting rounds.
The cards dealt face down to one player, seen only by them. Two in hold'em, four in Omaha.
Cards dealt face up in the middle of the table that every player uses in their hand. In hold'em there are five: the flop, turn and river.
The community cards on the table at any point in a hand, as in 'the board is K 7 2'.
The first betting round of a hold'em hand, after the hole cards are dealt and before any community cards.
The first three community cards in hold'em, dealt together, and the betting round after them. As a verb, to flop a hand is to make it with those cards.
The fourth community card in hold'em, and the betting round after it. Also called fourth street.
The fifth and last community card in hold'em, and the final betting round after it. Also called fifth street.
The end of a hand when two or more players remain after the last betting round: they show their cards and the best hand wins the pot.
The smaller of the two forced bets posted before the cards are dealt, by the player to the dealer's left (by the dealer, heads-up); usually half a big blind. Also the seat that posts it.
The larger forced bet, posted by the second player to the dealer's left before the cards are dealt. Stakes, stacks and win rates are measured in big blinds (bb).
A small forced bet taken from every player (or, as a big-blind ante, from one player for the whole table) before a hand, to make the pot bigger. Common in tournaments.
The disc marking the nominal dealer, who acts last after the flop. It moves one seat clockwise every hand. Also the seat itself, the best position at the table.
To decline to bet while keeping the hand, passing the action on. Only possible when nobody has bet on this round.
To match the current bet and stay in the hand.
To increase the current bet. Others must then match the larger amount, raise again or fold.
To give up a hand and any chips already put into the pot.
Having put every chip you have into the pot. A player all-in for less than a bet can only win that much from each other player; the rest goes to a side pot.
A separate pot made by the chips a short-stacked all-in player cannot match. Only the players who put chips into it can win it.
A pot shared equally between players whose hands tie exactly. Also called a chop.
The first raise of a hand before the flop, also called an open. Entering a pot by raising rather than calling is standard in modern play.
To enter the pot before the flop by just calling the big blind rather than raising. Mostly a sign of a weak player, except from the small blind.
A betting structure in which a player may bet any amount up to all their chips at any time.
A betting structure in which the largest bet or raise is the size of the pot, counting the call. The usual structure for Omaha.
A betting structure with bets and raises in fixed sizes: a small bet on the first two rounds and a big bet on the last two, usually capped at four bets per round.
A poker game played for chips worth real money, which players can join, leave and buy into at any time. Also called a ring game.
The chips a player has in front of them, usually measured in big blinds.
The order of poker hands from best to worst: royal flush, straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card.
A-K-Q-J-T all of one suit: the best possible hand in standard poker, the highest straight flush.
Five cards in sequence, all of one suit. Only 40 of the 2,598,960 five-card hands, including the four royal flushes.
Four cards of the same rank, such as four queens. Also called quads.
Three cards of one rank and two of another. Ranked first by the three of a kind: kings full of fours beats queens full of aces.
Five cards of the same suit, not in sequence. Compared by the highest card, then the next.
Five cards of consecutive rank in more than one suit. The ace can play high (A-K-Q-J-T, Broadway) or low (5-4-3-2-A, the wheel).
Three cards of one rank. Made with a pocket pair and one board card it is a set; with one hole card and a pair on the board it is trips.
Two cards of one rank, two of another and a fifth card.
An unpaired side card that decides between hands of the same kind: with A-K against A-Q on an ace-high board, the king kicker wins.
5-4-3-2-A, the lowest straight; also the best hand in ace-to-five lowball.
The first seat to act before the flop, just left of the big blind. The worst position preflop, so it plays the fewest hands.
The seat to the right of the button, the second-best position at the table.
The seat two to the right of the button, before the cutoff.
The seat three to the right of the button, before the hijack. In six-handed games it is the first to act, often called UTG.
Acting after a given opponent on the flop, turn and river, an advantage on every street because you see their action first.
Acting before a given opponent on the flop, turn and river, which makes every decision harder.
A form of poker with four hole cards, of which a hand must use exactly two with exactly three community cards. Usually played pot-limit (PLO).
A form of poker with no community cards: each player gets seven cards of their own, some face up, over five betting rounds.
Forms of poker in which the lowest hand wins, such as ace-to-five (Razz) and deuce-to-seven (2-7 triple draw).

Split-pot poker in which the best high hand and the best qualifying low hand (five cards of different ranks, all eight or lower) each win half the pot; with no qualifying low, the high hand takes it all. Winning both halves is scooping.
Hold'em played with the 2s to 5s removed, leaving 36 cards, so a flush beats a full house. Also called six-plus hold'em.
One specific pair of hole cards, such as AhKd, often called a combo. There are 1,326 in all: 6 for each pocket pair, 4 for each suited hand and 12 for each offsuit hand.
The hole cards a player is dealt. Hold'em has 169 kinds of starting hand (13 pairs, 78 suited and 78 offsuit) made from 1,326 combinations.
Two hole cards of the same rank, such as 7-7. One hand in 17 is a pocket pair.
Of two hole cards: the same suit, written with an s (AKs). Suited hands can make flushes, worth a few percent of equity.
Of two hole cards: different suits, written with an o (AKo).
Suited hole cards of consecutive rank, such as 8-7 suited. They make straights and flushes and play well in deep-stacked pots.
The cards ten through ace, which make the highest straight (A-K-Q-J-T, Broadway).
The effect of the cards you can see on which combinations an opponent can hold: holding an ace leaves only three combos of AA.
A card in your hand that makes certain hands impossible or less likely for an opponent, such as the ace of the flush suit blocking the nut flush.
The unseen cards that would turn a hand that is behind into the best hand.
A shortcut for drawing odds: on the flop, outs times 4 is roughly the percentage chance of hitting by the river; on the turn, outs times 2 is the chance on the river.
Four cards of one suit, needing one more to make a flush: 9 outs, about 35% to get there from the flop to the river.
Four cards in a row that can be completed at either end, such as 8-7-6-5: 8 outs, about 31.5% from the flop.
A straight draw that needs one inside card, such as 9-8-6-5 needing a 7: 4 outs, about 16.5% from the flop. Also called an inside straight draw.
A hand with two draws at once, typically a flush draw with a straight draw. With 15 outs on the flop it is a slight favourite (about 54%) even against a made hand.
A draw that needs both the turn and river cards, such as a backdoor flush. Worth about one out: around 4% for a backdoor flush.
Three of a kind made with a pocket pair and one matching board card. A pocket pair flops a set or better about 11.8% of the time.
Three of a kind made with one hole card and a pair on the board. Weaker than a set, because the third card is easy for others to share.
A card higher than any on the board, or higher than a pocket pair. AK on a flop of 8-6-2 has two overcards, about 6 outs.
A pocket pair higher than every card on the board, such as QQ on J-7-3.
A pair made with the highest card on the board.
An all-in between two hands with close to equal equity, classically a pocket pair against two higher cards (22 against AK, about 53% to 47%).
A hand is dominated when it shares a card with a better hand, as AQ is with AK: it wins only about a quarter of the time.
A hand's share of the pot if it were played to the end with no more betting: its chance of winning plus half its chance of tying.
Losing a hand in which you were a big favourite when the money went in.
A hand in which a strong hand meets a stronger one and big losses are unavoidable, such as KK against AA preflop.
The ratio of the pot to the cost of a call. A call needs at least call / (pot after the call) equity to break even: 25% against a half-pot bet, 33% against a pot-sized one.
The average result of a decision over every way it could turn out, weighted by probability. Poker skill is choosing the action with the highest EV.
Pot odds that also count what you expect to win on later streets if your draw comes in. They justify calls with set-mining hands and draws when stacks are deep.
The extra you expect to lose on later streets when your hand improves to a second-best hand, such as a low flush against a higher one.
The part of a bet's value that comes from the opponent folding. Gives semi-bluffs and short-stack shoves their profit.
A bet or raise with a hand that is probably behind but can improve to the best hand, such as a flush draw. It wins when they fold and sometimes when called.
A bet or raise with a weak hand, meant to make better hands fold.
The break-even fold frequency of a bluff: a bet b into a pot p must work b / (p + b) of the time. A pot-sized bluff needs 50%.
The share of a range, p / (p + b), a player must continue with against a bet of b into a pot p so that a bluff can't profit automatically: 50% against a pot-sized bet.
The smaller of the stacks between two players, the most either can win or lose against the other.
The effective stack divided by the pot on the flop. Low SPR makes one-pair hands strong enough to commit; high SPR favours hands that can make the nuts.
Having so much of a stack in the pot that calling the rest is profitable with almost any equity, because of the pot odds, not the money already spent.
The fee the house takes from each pot, usually a percentage up to a cap. Rakeback returns some of it.
Calling with a small pocket pair mainly to flop a set, which happens about 1 time in 8.5. Pays only with enough implied odds.
Results with each all-in hand counted at its expected value when the money went in instead of its actual outcome, removing the luck of the run-out.
Where a player sits relative to the dealer button, and so when they act. Acting last is a big advantage; see in position and out of position.
The set of hands a player raises with when first into the pot from a given seat; it widens from about 15% under the gun to 40% or more on the button.
The first re-raise before the flop (the big blind counts as the first bet and the open as the second). Usually about 3 times the open in position and 4 times out of position.
A re-raise of a 3-bet, usually about 2.2 to 2.5 times its size. With 100 big blinds it often commits the player to the pot.
A 3-bet after an open and one or more callers, whose calls suggest hands too weak to 3-bet.
Calling a raise without any money already in the pot.
A bet on the flop by the player who made the last raise before it.
Checking, then raising after an opponent bets. A strong play out of position with very strong hands and semi-bluffs.
A bet into the player who was the aggressor on the previous street, from out of position. Also called a lead.
Calling a bet in position with a weak hand, planning to take the pot later when the opponent shows weakness.
A bet on the turn from out of position after the preflop aggressor checked behind on the flop.
A bet on a later street after betting the one before. Betting flop, turn and river is a triple barrel.
Checking or calling with a very strong hand to hide its strength and let the opponent bet or catch up.
Checking or calling with a medium-strength hand to keep the pot small.
A bet bigger than the pot, used with a polarised range when you hold more of the nuts than the opponent.
A bet made to get called by worse hands. A thin value bet is one only slightly ahead of the hands that call.
How a board's cards connect with each other and with likely hands: dry boards have few draws, wet (dynamic) boards many; paired and monotone boards change which hands are strong.
Betting the same fraction of the pot on each remaining street so that the stacks go in exactly by the river.
The chance a hand wins if the hand is checked down to showdown. Hands with showdown value often check rather than bet or bluff.
Adjusting to an opponent's mistakes to win more from them, at the cost of becoming exploitable yourself.
A player who plays few hands and plays them mostly by betting and raising. The usual winning style.
A player who plays many hands, aggressively.
A very tight player who plays few hands and rarely bluffs.
A player who calls too much and rarely raises or folds. Value-bet them thinly and don't bluff them.
A weak, usually recreational player.
A player who bets and raises with almost any hand.
Choosing which games to play by the weakness of the opponents in them, one of the biggest sources of a winning player's profit.
Software that shows statistics on each opponent at an online table, built from a database of past hands.
Voluntarily put money in pot: the share of hands in which a player calls or raises before the flop, not counting forced blinds. A measure of how loose they are.
Preflop raise: the share of hands a player raises before the flop.
After the flop, bets plus raises divided by calls. High numbers mean an aggressive player.
Went to showdown: the share of hands that saw the flop in which a player went to showdown. High numbers mark a calling station.
A behaviour that gives away information about a player's hand, such as acting fast, a change in posture or a pattern of bet sizes.
Playing worse because of emotion, usually after bad beats or losses.
Judging a decision by how it turned out instead of by its expected value.
Thinking about what an opponent thinks you hold, and what they think you think, and so on.
Every hand a player could hold in a spot, each weighted by how likely it is. Players read and plan in ranges, not single hands.
A range that mixes strong hands and bluffs (and protects its checks with some strong hands) in proportions that leave nothing to exploit.
A range of very strong hands and bluffs with few medium hands, suited to large bets.
A range of the strongest hands down to a cut-off, also called merged, suited to smaller bets that get called by slightly worse hands.
A range of mostly medium-strength hands, such as a calling range, which struggles against big bets.
A range that can't contain the strongest hands, because with them the player would have raised earlier.
Having more equity across your whole range than the opponent does across theirs on a given board. It favours betting often.
Having more of the very strongest hands than the opponent on a given board. It allows large bets and overbets.
The best possible hand given the board. The nut flush is the best possible flush.
A hand that beats only bluffs and loses to every value bet; its decision to call depends only on how often the opponent bluffs.
A poker strategy that is a Nash equilibrium (or close to one): it can't be exploited, so in two-player zero-sum games it loses nothing in expectation from a symmetric position against any opponent.
How much a perfect counter-strategy would win against a strategy. A Nash equilibrium has zero exploitability.
Playing the same hand in more than one way at set frequencies, such as betting 60% and checking 40%, as equilibrium strategies often do.
At equilibrium, a player mixes between two actions only when they have equal EV, and the opponent's frequencies are set to make them so. The source of equilibrium bluffing and calling frequencies.
A toy poker game with a three-card deck used to show equilibrium bluffing and calling: the bettor bluffs the queen one time in three and the caller calls with the king one time in three.
A simplified version of poker, small enough to solve by hand, used to show equilibrium ideas.
The share of its raw equity a hand actually wins, given the betting to come. In position and suited hands realise more; out of position and offsuit ones less.
A program that computes an approximate Nash equilibrium for a poker situation defined by ranges, board, stacks and allowed bet sizes.

An algorithm that finds approximate equilibria by self-play: it repeatedly shifts the strategy at every decision towards the actions it most regrets not taking. Its average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games.
Fixing an opponent's strategy at one decision in a solver and computing the best response to it, to find exploitative adjustments.
Grouping similar hands, cards or bet sizes into one in order to make a game small enough to solve.
Sklansky's principle: whenever you play a hand differently from how you would if you could see the opponents' cards, they gain; whenever you play it the same way, you gain.
A poker event where everyone starts with equal chips, blinds rise on a schedule and players are knocked out; prizes go to the last few by finishing place.
A model that turns tournament stacks into shares of the prize pool by assuming each player finishes first with their share of the chips, then second among the rest in the same way, and so on.
The point in a tournament just before the paid places, when one more elimination puts every remaining player in the money.
The prize equity a player loses by losing an all-in, divided by what they gain by winning it. A bubble factor of 2 means an even-money all-in needs 67% equity.
The extra equity, above the chip-EV break-even, that ICM makes a tournament player need to call an all-in.
Expected value measured in tournament chips rather than prize money. Close to money EV early in a tournament, far from it near the money.
Expected value measured in prize money, the thing a tournament player wants to maximise; ICM estimates it from stacks.
The short-stack strategy of either going all in or folding, close to optimal below about 15 big blinds. Nash push-fold charts give the shoving and calling ranges.
Harrington's measure of a tournament stack: chips divided by the cost of one round of blinds and antes, the number of orbits a player could survive without playing.
The last table of a multi-table tournament, where the biggest prize jumps are.
A deal among the last players of a tournament that splits the remaining prize money by ICM equity. A chip chop splits by chip share instead, favouring the leader.
A bounty tournament in which half of a busted player's bounty goes to the eliminator at once and half is added to the eliminator's own bounty.
A tournament whose prizes are seats in a bigger tournament. Since every seat is worth the same, ICM pressure near the bubble is extreme.
A tournament that starts as soon as enough players have registered, often a single table.
A cash-game player's average profit, usually in big blinds per 100 hands (bb/100).
How widely a poker player's results swing, usually measured in big blinds per 100 hands. Typically 60 to 100 bb/100 in no-limit hold'em.
The swings of results around their expected value caused by luck. In poker it is large: winning players routinely lose for tens of thousands of hands.
A stretch of losing results. Downswings of 10 to 20 buy-ins are ordinary even for strong cash-game players.
The chance a bankroll is lost entirely before it grows. For win rate w, standard deviation s and bankroll B (in the same units) it is about exp(-2wB/s²) at fixed stakes.
The money set aside for playing poker, measured in buy-ins of the stake played.
Rules for which stakes to play for a given bankroll, such as keeping 20 to 50 buy-ins for cash games and many more for tournaments, to keep the risk of going broke low.
The amount a player pays to enter a tournament, or brings to a cash game; 100 big blinds is the usual cash-game buy-in.
A tournament player's profit divided by their total buy-ins.
The number of hands (or tournaments) behind a result or statistic. Poker needs large samples: about 100,000 hands narrow a win rate only to about plus or minus 6 bb/100.
The staking rule that maximises the long-run growth rate of a bankroll; it says to risk a small share of the bankroll when the edge is small relative to the variance.
Finished, or still playing, in a paid place of a tournament: past the bubble.
Interest earned on earlier interest as well as on the original sum, so growth accelerates over time: FV = PV(1 + r)^n.
Interest paid only on the original sum, never on interest already earned.
What a sum invested today grows to after a number of periods at a given rate.
What a future payment is worth today, found by discounting it at the rate you could earn elsewhere: PV = CF / (1 + r)^n.
The rate used to turn future cash into present value; it reflects the return available on investments of similar risk.
The present value of an investment's future cash flows minus its cost today; positive means it earns more than the discount rate.
The discount rate that makes an investment's net present value zero; for a bond it is the yield to maturity.
A series of equal payments at regular intervals, such as loan payments or bond coupons; also an insurance product that pays income for life or a set term.
A stream of payments that lasts forever, worth C / r, or C1 / (r − g) if it grows at rate g.
The rate actually earned in a year once compounding within the year is counted: (1 + r/m)^m − 1.
A loan's quoted yearly rate, usually without the effect of compounding within the year.
A shortcut: money doubles in about 72 / r years at r percent a year.
Paying off a loan through regular payments that cover interest and part of the principal; also the gradual writing-down of an intangible asset in accounts.
Return after inflation: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1, about nominal minus inflation.
Return in money terms, before adjusting for inflation.
The link between nominal and real rates: 1 + nominal = (1 + real)(1 + inflation).
The constant yearly rate that would turn a starting value into an ending value over the period; the geometric average of returns.
The gap between average and compound returns caused by volatility, roughly σ²/2 a year.
Price change plus income (dividends or interest), as a share of the starting price.
A return that chains sub-period returns and ignores the size and timing of deposits and withdrawals; how funds report performance.
The internal rate of return on an investor's actual cash flows, which reflects when money was added or taken out.
Where new securities are sold by their issuer to investors, as in an IPO or a bond auction.
Where investors trade existing securities with each other, as on a stock exchange.
A company's first sale of shares to the public, after which they trade on an exchange.
The gap between the highest price a buyer will pay (bid) and the lowest a seller will take (ask); a cost of trading.
A dealer who continuously quotes prices to buy and sell a security, earning the spread.
Trading directly between dealers and clients rather than through a central exchange; most bonds, currencies and swaps trade this way.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price.
An order to buy at no more than, or sell at no less than, a set price.
An order that becomes a market order once the price reaches a trigger level; it may fill well below the trigger in a fast market.
The exchange of cash for securities after a trade; one business day after the trade for US stocks since 2024.
A brokerage account that lets you borrow against your holdings to buy more, magnifying gains and losses.
A demand to add cash or securities when losses push equity below the required minimum; if unmet the position is sold.
Selling borrowed shares in the hope of buying them back cheaper; the possible loss is unlimited.
A rapid price rise forced by short sellers buying back to limit their losses.
Share price times shares outstanding: the market value of a company's equity.
The shares available for public trading, excluding large holdings by insiders and governments; most indexes weight by it.
An index of about 500 large US companies weighted by market value; the usual benchmark for US stocks.
A price-weighted index of 30 large US companies, first published in 1896.
Global stock indexes from MSCI: World covers developed markets; ACWI (All Country World Index) adds emerging markets.
A US tax-advantaged retirement account: traditional IRAs give a deduction now and tax withdrawals; Roth IRAs tax contributions and make qualified withdrawals tax-free.
A US employer retirement plan funded from pay before (or, for Roth 401(k)s, after) tax, often with an employer match.
A UK account in which savings and investments grow free of income and capital gains tax, up to a yearly allowance.
Money an employer adds to a retirement plan in proportion to the employee's contributions.
Cash set aside for unexpected expenses, typically three to six months of spending, so investments need not be sold at a bad time.
A cash payment from a company's profits to its shareholders.
A year's dividends divided by the share price.
The first day a stock trades without the right to its next dividend; the price usually drops by about the dividend.
Dividends as a share of earnings.
A company buying its own shares, returning cash to sellers and raising remaining owners' share of the company.
Dividing each share into several, lowering the price per share without changing the company's value.
Shares that pay a fixed dividend ahead of common dividends and rank above common stock in bankruptcy, usually without votes.
Ordinary ownership shares, with votes and a residual claim on profits after everyone else is paid.
A certificate traded in the US that represents shares of a foreign company.
A fall in existing owners' share of a company when new shares are issued.
Size groups by market value: large-cap roughly above \$10 billion, mid-cap \$2 to 10 billion, small-cap \$300 million to \$2 billion.
A stock expected to grow earnings quickly, usually priced at a high multiple of current earnings.
A stock priced cheaply relative to its earnings, book value or cash flow.
A stock whose profits rise and fall with the economy; defensive stocks sell necessities and hold up better in downturns.
The system that sorts listed companies into 11 sectors and finer industry groups.
The annual report a US public company files with the SEC; the 10-Q is its quarterly counterpart.
The SEC's free online database of US company filings.
The US accounting rules; non-GAAP figures are company-adjusted measures that exclude some items.
The accounting rules used by listed companies in most countries outside the US.
The statement of revenue, costs and profit over a period.
A snapshot of what a company owns (assets) and owes (liabilities), with shareholders' equity as the difference.
The statement that reconciles profit to the actual change in cash, split into operating, investing and financing flows.
The money a company takes in from selling goods and services, before costs.
Revenue minus the cost of goods sold, as a share of revenue.
Operating income (EBIT) as a share of revenue.
Profit after all expenses, interest and taxes.
Earnings before interest and taxes: profit from operations regardless of how the company is financed.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; a rough measure of operating cash generation that ignores the cost of replacing assets.
Net income divided by shares outstanding.
Spreading the cost of equipment and buildings over their useful lives as an expense.
The premium paid for an acquisition above the fair value of its identifiable assets, carried on the balance sheet.
Assets minus liabilities as recorded in the accounts; what owners would get if everything sold at book values.
Current assets minus current liabilities; changes in it make cash flow differ from profit.
Money spent on long-term assets such as equipment and buildings.
Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure: cash the business produces beyond what it needs to sustain and grow itself.
Net income divided by shareholders' equity.
After-tax operating profit divided by the capital invested in the business (debt plus equity minus cash).
Splitting ROE into net margin × asset turnover × leverage to see where it comes from.
EBIT divided by interest expense: how easily a company pays its interest.
Debt minus cash; often compared with EBITDA to gauge leverage.
The part of earnings not yet received or paid in cash; high accruals have predicted weaker future returns.
Share price divided by earnings per share: what investors pay for a dollar of yearly profit.
Earnings per share divided by price, the inverse of the P/E.
The P/E divided by the expected earnings growth rate in percent.
Market capitalization divided by book value.
Market capitalization plus debt minus cash (and other claims): the value of the whole business, used in EV/EBITDA comparisons.
Price divided by the average of ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings; high values have preceded lower long-run returns.
Value = next year's dividend / (required return − growth), for dividends growing at a constant rate forever.
Valuing a business as the present value of its expected future free cash flows plus a terminal value.
In a DCF, the value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast years, usually by the Gordon formula.
The blended required return on a company's debt (after tax) and equity, used to discount its free cash flows.
The return shareholders require, often estimated with CAPM.
Solving for the growth that today's price implies, instead of computing a value from a forecast.
Buying well below estimated value so that errors in the estimate don't cause a loss.
A durable competitive advantage that protects a company's profits from rivals.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest (coupons) and returns the principal at maturity.
The amount a bond repays at maturity, usually 100 per 100 or \$1,000.
A bond's yearly interest payment as a percentage of face value.
The date a bond's principal is repaid.
A bond that pays no coupons and is sold below face value; its return is the rise to par.
A bond the issuer may repay early, usually when rates have fallen.
The single discount rate that makes a bond's cash flows equal its price; its return if held to maturity with coupons reinvested at that rate.
A bond's yearly coupon divided by its price.
The lowest yield a bond can give across every date the issuer could repay it.
Coupon interest earned since the last payment, paid by a bond's buyer on top of the quoted clean price.
A bond's price sensitivity to yields: price falls about D% for each 1-point rise in yield. Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to its cash flows.
The curvature of a bond's price-yield relation; positive convexity means gains from falling yields exceed losses from equal rises.
The change in a bond's value for a one-basis-point (0.01%) change in yield.
One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%).
A set of bonds maturing in successive years, giving regular repayments and smoothing interest-rate risk.
The risk that coupons and maturing bonds must be reinvested at lower rates.
US government zero-coupon debt maturing within a year; the usual measure of the risk-free rate.
US government coupon debt: notes mature in 2 to 10 years, bonds in 20 or 30.
US Treasury bonds whose principal rises with inflation, giving a known real yield.
US savings bonds sold to individuals, paying a fixed rate plus an inflation rate; they cannot lose value.
The nominal Treasury yield minus the TIPS yield of the same maturity: the inflation rate at which both return the same.
UK government bonds.
German federal government bonds, the benchmark for the euro area.
Bonds issued by the Japanese government.
A bond issued by a US state, city or local agency; interest is usually exempt from federal income tax.
The taxable yield that would match a tax-free yield after tax: tax-free yield / (1 − tax rate).
A bond backed by a pool of home loans, whose payments pass through to investors.
Bonds issued by a national government.
A rating agency's grade of a borrower's ability to pay, from AAA down to D.
Bonds rated BBB−/Baa3 or higher.
